A Growing People

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 1: Explain the major factors that contributed to the demographic changes in the British American colonies during the eighteenth century.

Core Objective 2: Describe the various roles of White and enslaved women in the British American colonies.

IN MY WORDS: In your own words, why did the colonies grow so fast, and what work did women do?

Reading AThe Population Booms

Once colonial life became more settled, however, the population grew rapidly. On average, it doubled every twenty-five years. By 1750, the number of colonists had passed 1 million; by 1775, it approached 2.5 million. . . . Benjamin Franklin, a keen observer of life in British America, said that the colonial population grew so rapidly because land was plentiful and cheap, and laborers were scarce and costly.

Colonists tended to marry and start families at an earlier age than was common in Europe. . . . High rates of immigration from Europe to the British American colonies across the eighteenth century continued to drive the overall population upward.

Word help: rapidly = fast · doubled = became two times as big · scarce = hard to find · immigration = people moving in from other countries

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “The Demography of the Early Colonies” (Population Growth; Birth and Death Rates; Immigrants and Citizenship).

Reading B“Women’s Work”

White women, as had been true for centuries, were expected to focus on “housewifery,” or the “domestic sphere.” They were to obey and serve their husbands, nurture their children, and maintain their households. . . . Women in most colonies could not vote, own property, hold office, attend schools or colleges, bring lawsuits, sign contracts, or become ministers.

In the eighteenth century, women’s work typically centered on activities in the house, garden, and fields. . . . They fed and watered the livestock, cared for the children, tended the garden, prepared lunch (the main meal) and dinner, milked the cows, and cleaned the kitchen before retiring soon after dark.

Word help: housewifery = running a home · domestic sphere = the home and family · nurture = care for · lawsuits = cases in court · livestock = farm animals

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “Women in the Colonies” (“Women’s Work”).

Reading CEnslaved Women and Eliza Lucas Pinckney

Enslaved women worked from before sunrise to after dark. . . . Enslaved women in agricultural settings cultivated crops such as tobacco, cotton, sugar, wheat, corn, potatoes, and other vegetables. . . . Their labor supported White families, particularly those wealthy enough to afford enslaved laborers.

On occasion, circumstances forced women to exercise leadership outside the home. Such was the case with South Carolinian Elizabeth (“Eliza”) Lucas Pinckney (1722–1793). . . . Eliza Pinckney demonstrated the possibility of White women breaking out of the confining tradition of housewifery and subordination and assuming roles of social prominence and economic leadership—work that was accomplished with the help of an enslaved workforce.

Word help: on call = ready to work at any time · agricultural = farm · cultivated = grew · subordination = being under someone’s control · prominence = importance

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “Women in the Colonies” (Enslaved Women; Eliza Lucas Pinckney and Plantation Management).

Part 2 of 7

Three Colonial Regions

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 3: Compare the societies and economies of the southern, New England, and middle colonies, and describe the roles of indentured servants, enslaved Indigenous people, and enslaved Africans.

IN MY WORDS: Who did the hardest work in the colonies? Name two groups.

Reading DServants and Enslaved Native Americans

To solve the labor shortage, the planters first recruited indentured servants from England, Ireland, Scotland, and continental Europe. The term derived from the indenture, or contract, that enabled a person to pay for passage to America by promising to work for a fixed number of years (usually between three and seven). . . . The most important difference between servanthood and slavery was that the former did not last a lifetime.

In Carolina, as many as 50,000 Indigenous people, mostly women and children, were sold into slavery in Charles Town between 1670 and 1715. . . . By the early eighteenth century, however, traders in the Carolinas would come to prefer enslaved Africans over enslaved Native Americans.

Word help: labor shortage = not enough workers · planters = owners of big farms · contract = a written deal · passage = the trip by ship · the former = the first one (servanthood)

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “Society and Economy in the Colonies” (Indentured Servitude; The Trade in Enslaved Native Americans).

Reading EThe Southern Colonies

In the southern colonies, inequalities of wealth and status became more visible. The use of enslaved Indigenous and African people to grow tobacco, sugar cane, rice, and indigo generated enormous wealth for a few landowners. . . . Warm weather and plentiful rainfall helped the southern colonies grow the profitable staple crops valued by Great Britain. . . . As rice plantations grew, the demand for enslaved laborers rose dramatically, for White colonists balked at working long hours in “mud and water.” Almost 90 percent of the enslaved Africans transported to America were sold into the southern colonies.

Word help: inequalities = big differences · status = rank in society · staple crops = main crops grown to sell · balked = refused

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “Society and Economy in the Colonies” (The Southern Colonies).

Reading FNew England and the Triangular Trade

New England was quite different from the southern and middle Atlantic regions. . . . Commercial agriculture was almost nonexistent because of the rocky soil and frigid climate, so traders and shopkeepers predominated.

These circumstances gave rise to the triangular trade. New England merchants shipped rum to the western coast of Africa, where it was exchanged for captured and enslaved Africans. Ships then took the captive Africans to profitable Caribbean islands to sell. . . . The ships returned home with various commodities, including molasses, from which New Englanders manufactured rum.

Word help: commercial agriculture = farming to sell crops · frigid = very cold · predominated = were the main group · commodities = goods · molasses = a sweet syrup made from sugarcane

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “Society and Economy in the Colonies” (New England).

Reading GThe Middle Colonies

Both geographically and culturally, the middle colonies (New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, and Maryland) stood between New England and the South. As such, they more completely reflected the diversity of colonial life and more fully foreshadowed the pluralism of America. . . . By the mid-eighteenth century, the middle colonies were the fastest-growing region in North America. Pennsylvania became the great distribution point for the ethnic groups of European origin.

Word help: diversity = many kinds of people · foreshadowed = showed early signs of · pluralism = many groups living together · ethnic groups = groups with the same language and culture

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “Society and Economy in the Colonies” (The Middle Colonies).

Part 3 of 7

Race-Based Slavery

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Describe the creation of race-based chattel slavery during the seventeenth century and its impact on the social and economic development of colonial America.

IN MY WORDS: What does it mean that slavery became “race-based” and lasted “for life”?

Reading HThe Middle Passage

The transport of African captives, mostly young men, across the Atlantic to the Americas was the largest forced migration in world history. . . . The transatlantic voyage of the slave ships, which could last up to six months, was known as the Middle Passage because it served as the middle leg of the triangular trade. . . . The Middle Passage was horrific. One in six African captives died along the way.

Once they arrived in America, Africans were treated as property (chattel), herded in chains to public auctions, and sold to the highest bidder.

Word help: captives = prisoners · forced migration = people made to move against their will · transatlantic voyage = trip across the Atlantic Ocean · horrific = terrible · auctions = sales to whoever pays most

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “Society and Economy in the Colonies” (African Roots and the Middle Passage; Africans as Property).

Picture 1Diagram of a Slave Ship

This diagram was published in the United States around 1808. It shows how enslaved Africans were packed below deck on a slave ship. (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: Fig. = figure, one drawing · deck = a floor of a ship · the rows of small dark shapes = enslaved people lying down · Store Room = where supplies were kept

Norton, Ch. 3, “Society and Economy in the Colonies,” caption: “Slave Ship. One in six Africans died from the brutal and cramped conditions while crossing the Atlantic in ships like this one, from an American diagram ca. 1808.” Primary source.

Picture 1. Describe how the people are placed on this ship. Use Reading H: how does this help explain why one in six captives died?

Reading IFrom Servant to Slave for Life

In the Chesapeake colonies of Virginia and Maryland, Africans were initially treated much like indentured servants—with a limited term of service, after which they gained their freedom (but not equality). By the 1640s, however, slavery had become a permanent and hereditary condition determined by race.

The case of John Punch (1641) marked one of the origins of racial slavery. Punch, an indentured servant from Africa, ran away with two other servants—a Scotsman named James Gregory and a Dutchman named Victor. . . . However, when caught, James and Victor received an extension of their indentured service for a few extra years. Punch, because he was African, was punished with slavery for the rest of his “natural life.” This case revealed how colonial legislatures formalized the institution of race-based chattel slavery, with detailed slave codes regulating most aspects of enslaved people’s lives.

Word help: moveable property = things that can be owned and moved, like animals · moral issue = a question of right and wrong · initially = at first · hereditary = passed from parents to children · legislatures = groups that make laws · slave codes = laws that controlled enslaved people

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “Race-Based Chattel Slavery in the Colonies” (Differing Treatment of Enslaved Africans; Slave Codes).

Reading JThe Stono Rebellion (1739)

On Sunday morning, September 9, 1739, while White families were attending church, some twenty African-born enslaved people attacked a store in Stono, South Carolina, twenty miles southwest of Charles Town. . . . Within a few days, the Stono rebels had burned six plantations and killed about two dozen Whites.

The Stono Rebellion, the largest uprising of the colonial period, so frightened White planters that they convinced the South Carolina assembly to ban the importation of enslaved Africans for ten years. . . . Enslaved people could no longer grow their own food, gather in groups, learn to read or write, or earn money on the side.

Word help: rebels = people who fight against those in power · militiamen = part-time citizen soldiers · uprising = a revolt · assembly = a colony’s law-making group · importation = bringing in from another place

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “Race-Based Chattel Slavery in the Colonies” (Freedom Seekers and Slave Rebellions).

Part 4 of 7

New Ideas: Reason and Revival

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 5: Analyze the impact of the Enlightenment and Great Awakening on American religious thought during the colonial period.

IN MY WORDS: One movement trusted the head (reason). One trusted the heart (feelings). Which was which?

Reading KThe Enlightenment

The most significant of the new European ideas circulating in eighteenth-century America grew out of a burst of intellectual activity known as the Enlightenment. The Enlightenment celebrated rational inquiry, scientific research, and individual freedom. . . . Some enlightened people, called Deists, carried Newton’s scientific outlook to its logical conclusion, claiming that God created the world and designed its natural laws, which governed the operation of the universe.

Both Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Franklin were intrigued by the writings of English political philosopher John Locke, who maintained that “natural law” called for a government that rested on the consent of the governed and respected the “natural rights” of all.

Word help: rational inquiry = asking questions and using reason · Newton = a scientist who explained gravity · natural laws = rules of nature, like gravity · consent of the governed = the people agree to the government · natural rights = rights every person is born with

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “First Stirrings of a Common Colonial Culture” (The Enlightenment).

Reading LThe Great Awakening

The growing popularity of Enlightenment rationalism posed a direct threat to traditional religious life. But in the early eighteenth century, the American colonies experienced a revival of spiritual zeal designed to restore the primacy of emotion in the religious realm. . . . During the early 1730s, these itinerant preachers helped spark a series of revivals known as the Great Awakening. . . . The highly emotional gatherings divided congregations, towns, and families; they even fueled popular new denominations, especially Baptists and Methodists.

Edwards rushed to restore the emotional side of religion. “Our people,” he said, “do not so much need to have their heads stored [with new scientific knowledge] as to have their hearts touched [with spiritual intensity].”

Word help: rationalism = trust in reason · revival = a burst of new religious feeling · zeal = strong feeling · primacy = first place · itinerant preachers = traveling preachers · Edwards = Jonathan Edwards, a minister in Massachusetts · congregations = church groups · denominations = branches of a religion

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 3, “First Stirrings of a Common Colonial Culture” (The Great Awakening; Jonathan Edwards).

Part 5 of 7

Two Empires and a World War

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 6: Compare how the British and French Empires administered their colonies before 1763.

Core Objective 7: Analyze how the French and Indian War changed relations among the European powers in North America.

IN MY WORDS: Who won the French and Indian War, and what did the winner gain?

Reading MNew France

By the mid-eighteenth century, the French residents of New France numbered less than 5 percent of the population in British America, and the relatively small French investment in Canada and Louisiana never turned a profit.

In 1627, the French monarchy announced that only French Catholics could live in New France. This restriction stunted the settlement’s growth—as did the harsh winter climate. . . . Champlain knew that the French could survive only by befriending the Indigenous peoples. To that end, he dispatched trappers and traders to live with them, learn their languages and customs, and marry their women.

Word help: New France = France’s colonies in Canada and along the Mississippi River · monarchy = the king’s government · stunted = slowed · Champlain = the French leader who founded New France · convert = change someone’s religion

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “French and British Colonies” (New France; Relations with Indigenous Societies; Catholicism and Jesuit Missionaries).

Reading NThe British Colonial System

Yet the British colonists enjoyed rights and powers absent in Britain and in New France. In particular, they had elected legislatures. . . . Self-government in British America became first a habit, then a cherished “right.”

As England’s new ruler, Cromwell sought to enforce mercantilism—a political and economic policy in which the government controlled economic activities. . . . The Navigation Act of 1651 required that all goods going to and from the colonies be transported in English-owned ships.

Word help: elected legislatures = law-making groups chosen by voters · cherished = deeply loved · Cromwell = the leader who ruled England in the 1650s · policy = a plan of action · transported = carried

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “French and British Colonies” (The British Colonial System; The Habit of Self-Government; Mercantilism; Navigation Acts).

Reading OThe Glorious Revolution (1688) and Salutary Neglect

People called the revolution “glorious” because it took place with little bloodshed. . . . The monarchy in England would never again exercise absolute power.

Soon, however, British efforts to enforce the Navigation Acts waned. . . . Robert Walpole, the long-serving prime minister (1721–1742) and lord of the Treasury, initiated a policy of salutary neglect. . . . What Walpole did not realize was that his policy of salutary neglect would lead many colonists to develop an independent attitude that would ultimately blossom into revolution.

Word help: bloodshed = killing · absolute power = total power with no limits · waned = got weaker · salutary neglect = a “healthy” habit of not enforcing the trade laws · rigid enforcement = strictly making people obey

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “French and British Colonies” (The Glorious Revolution; A New Emerging Colonial System).

Reading PThe French and Indian War

The most important conflict between Britain and France (and its Catholic ally, Spain) in North America was the French and Indian War (1756–1763), globally known as the Seven Years’ War. The conflict started with frontier clashes in America in 1754, sparked by French and British competition for the Indigenous lands in the vast Ohio valley.

The Treaty of Paris, signed in February 1763, gave Britain control of France’s territories east of the Mississippi River. . . . France itself was left with no territory on the North American continent, while Great Britain dramatically increased its imperial holdings and emerged as the greatest empire in the world . . . The staggering cost of maintaining the sprawling North American empire, including the permanent stationing of 10,000 British soldiers in the colonies, strained the imperial budget.

Word help: conflict = fight or war · frontier = the edge of settled land · compensation = payment for a loss · imperial holdings = lands in an empire · staggering = shockingly large · strained = put stress on

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “Warfare in the Colonies” (The French and Indian War; The Treaty of Paris (1763)).

Reading QPontiac’s Rebellion and the Proclamation Line

After the war, colonists grew eager to take ownership of Indigenous lands west of the Appalachian Mountains that the French had ceded to the British in the Treaty of Paris. . . . Pontiac told a British official that the “French never conquered us, neither did they purchase a foot of our Country, nor have they a right to give it to you.”

To help keep peace with the Indigenous nations, King George III issued the Proclamation Act of 1763, which drew an imaginary line along the crest of the Appalachian Mountains from Canada to Georgia (see again Map 4.4). . . . For the first time, royal officials were curtailing territorial expansion, and American colonists did not like it.

Word help: ceded = gave up · Pontiac = an Ottawa leader who fought British expansion · purchase = buy · crest = the top line of a mountain range · curtailing = cutting back · territorial expansion = taking more land

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “Warfare in the Colonies” (Pontiac’s Rebellion; The Proclamation Line).

MapMap 4.4: European Land Claims in North America, 1763

This modern textbook map shows who claimed North America after the Treaty of Paris (1763). The red line is the Proclamation Line of 1763.

Map key: Green = lands claimed by England · Pink = lands claimed by Spain · Red line = Proclamation Line of 1763 · Indian Reserve = land west of the line kept for Indigenous nations

Norton, Ch. 4, Map 4.4, “European Land Claims in North America, 1763.” Modern textbook map.

Part 6 of 7

From Protest to Independence

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 8: Describe how, after the French and Indian War, the British tightened their control over the colonies, and summarize the colonial responses.

Core Objective 9: Explain the underlying factors amid the events in the 1770s that led the colonists to declare their independence from Britain.

IN MY WORDS: What did colonists mean by “No taxation without representation”?

Reading RNew Taxes

Grenville insisted that American settlers pay for the British soldiers defending them. . . . With the Sugar Act, Parliament sought to raise revenues from the colonies and not merely to regulate their trade with other nations, as had been the case up to that point. Colonists claimed that the Sugar Act taxed them without their consent, since they had no elected representatives in Parliament.

The Stamp Act required colonists to purchase paper from London embossed with a government revenue stamp. . . . This law affected all colonists because it applied to paper for virtually every possible use: newspapers, pamphlets, deeds, licenses, insurance policies, college diplomas, even playing cards.

Word help: Grenville = Britain’s prime minister (head of government) · revenues = money from taxes · regulate = control with rules · consent = agreement · embossed = pressed with a raised design

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “Tightening of Control over the British Colonies” (Grenville’s Colonial Policy; The Sugar Act (1764); The Stamp Act (1765)).

Reading SPatriots Push Back

American colonists who opposed British policies began to call themselves Patriots, or Whigs, a name earlier applied to British critics of royal power. . . . In a flood of pamphlets, speeches, resolutions, and street protests, critics repeated a slogan familiar to American colonists: “No taxation without representation [in Parliament].”

Rebels, calling themselves Sons of Liberty, emerged in every colony to organize protests . . . Now, however, patriots by the thousands signed nonimportation (boycott) agreements pledging not to buy British goods. . . . The boycotts worked. . . . The growing rebellion in America convinced Rockingham that the Stamp Act was a mistake, and Parliament repealed it in February 1766.

Word help: opposed = were against · pamphlets = short printed booklets · slogan = a short saying · boycott = refusing to buy · Rockingham = Britain’s new prime minister · repealed = canceled

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “Tightening of Control over the British Colonies” (The Whig Point of View; Protests in the Colonies; The Nonimportation Movement; Colonial Unity; Repeal of the Stamp Act).

Reading TThe Townshend Acts and the Boston Massacre

The Revenue Act of 1767, which taxed colonial imports of glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea, was the most hated of the so-called Townshend Acts. . . . Loyalists, as the Americans who supported the king and Parliament had begun to be called, welcomed the soldiers; Patriots, those rebelling against British authority, viewed the troops as an occupation force.

A squad of soldiers arrived to help White, but the crowd surrounded them. When someone knocked a soldier down, he arose and fired his musket. Others joined in. After the smoke had cleared, five men lay dead or dying on the cobblestone street, and eight more were wounded. . . . The so-called Boston Massacre sent shock waves throughout the colonies and all the way to London.

Word help: imports = goods brought in from other countries · occupation force = enemy soldiers who control a place · squad = small group of soldiers · White = Hugh White, a British soldier guarding a building in Boston (March 5, 1770)

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “Tightening of Control over the British Colonies” (The Townshend Acts Fan the Flames). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “The Road to the American Revolution” (The Boston Massacre (1770)).

Reading UThe Boston Tea Party and the Coercive Acts

On December 16, 1773, scores of Patriots boarded three British cargo ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests filled with 46 tons of East India Company tea into the icy water.

In 1774, as a result of the Tea Party, Lord North convinced Parliament to punish Boston and the province of Massachusetts by passing a cluster of harsh laws, called the Coercive Acts. (Colonists renamed them the “Intolerable Acts.”) The Port Act closed Boston Harbor until the city paid for the lost tea. . . . Collectively, the Intolerable Acts outraged colonists and transformed scattered resistance into widespread rebellion.

Word help: scores = many (a score is 20) · forceful response = strong action · Lord North = Britain’s prime minister · coercive = forcing people to obey · intolerable = too much to put up with · collectively = all together

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “The Road to the American Revolution” (The Boston Tea Party (1773); The Coercive Acts).

Reading VCommon Sense and the Declaration of Independence

In January 1776, Paine published a stirring fifty-page pamphlet titled Common Sense, in which he urged Americans to seize their independence. . . . It convinced many anxious American rebels that independence was necessary and inevitable.

The more memorable date, however, became July 4, 1776, when fifty-six members of Congress formally adopted the Declaration of Independence creating the “United States of America.” . . . Southern representatives insisted on deleting Jefferson’s passage criticizing George III for imposing slavery on the colonies. In doing so, they revealed the major paradox at work in the movement for independence: the rhetoric of freedom (“all men are created equal and independent”) did not apply to the widespread system of slavery that fueled the colonial economy.

Word help: Paine = Thomas Paine, a writer who had recently moved to America · seize = grab · inevitable = sure to happen · Jefferson = Thomas Jefferson, who wrote the Declaration · paradox = something that contradicts itself · rhetoric = words used to persuade

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 4, “The Road to the American Revolution” (Independence; Breaking the Bonds of Empire (1776); The Contradictions of Freedom and Slavery).

Source 1“Remember the Ladies” (Primary Source)

Abigail Adams wrote this letter to her husband, John Adams, on March 31, 1776. He was a member of the Continental Congress, which was deciding whether to declare independence. The spelling is from 1776.

“I have sometimes been ready to think that the passion for Liberty cannot be equally strong in the breasts of those who have been accustomed to deprive their fellow creatures of theirs. . . . I long to hear that you have declared an independency—and by the way in the new Code of Laws which I suppose it will be necessary for you to make I desire you would remember the ladies and be more generous & favorable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power in the hands of the husbands. Remember all men would be tyrants if they could. If particular care and attention is not paid to the ladies, we are determined to foment a rebellion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any laws in which we have no voice or representation”

Word help: passion = strong feeling · breasts = hearts · deprive = take away from · fellow creatures = other people · Code of Laws = set of laws · tyrants = cruel rulers with total power · foment = stir up

Letter from Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776. In Norton, Ch. 4, “The Road to the American Revolution,” Comparing Perspectives: “On Coverture, Liberty, and Equality.”

CER: Freedom for Whom?

BIG QUESTION

Was colonial America a land of freedom—or only freedom for some?

Use the readings, Source 1, and the pictures in this assignment. Give two pieces of evidence. In the Counter-Argument box, explain what someone on the other side would say, and answer it.

ClaimAnswer the question in one sentence.
EvidenceTwo specific facts (dates, events, numbers).
ReasoningHow do the facts prove your claim?
Counter-ArgumentWhat would the other side say? Answer it.
